text: Ask a language model a simple question. The difference between a base model and a trained one is immediately visible.
First, text becomes token IDs. Synapse uses a sixty-four-thousand-token vocabulary, then maps every token into a two-thousand-five-hundred-sixty-dimensional vector.

Twenty-eight transformer blocks refine those vectors. Attention lets each position use earlier context, while SwiGLU layers transform what was retrieved. Rotary encoding tracks order, and grouped-query attention keeps inference efficient.
A final projection scores every possible next token. The model selects one, appends it, and repeats. An answer is simply many next-token decisions.

Pretraining teaches general text. Supervised fine-tuning adds conversations, but computes loss only on assistant responses, not the question. The same curated mix teaches instruction following, reasoning, formatting, and tool use.

On this sixteen-gigabyte laptop, full fine-tuning does not fit. LoRA freezes the two-point-one-billion-parameter base and learns small low-rank updates instead. The largest run trained three hundred three million adapter parameters, then merged them back for ordinary inference.
DPO adds preference learning. Curated answers are chosen, while corrupted or weaker base-model answers are rejected. This sharpens behavior without training a separate reward model.
The results are concrete: correct arithmetic, step-by-step change, algebra, and exact formatting. These are real generations from the validation dashboard, not handwritten answers.

Validation improved across every supervised source. Big LoRA reached one-point-one-nine-eight validation loss and seventy percent on the chat bench. DPO reached seventy-five. Same base. Better answers.
